answer_text:
Let the containers be labeled by their capacities: \(10\text{ l}, 5\text{ l}, 3\text{ l}\).  
Start with the \(10\text{ l}\) container full:

\[
(10,0,0)
\]

where the triple is \((10\text{ l container}, 5\text{ l container}, 3\text{ l container})\).

Now perform the following pours:

1. Pour from the \(10\text{ l}\) container into the \(5\text{ l}\) container:

\[
(5,5,0)
\]

2. Pour from the \(5\text{ l}\) container into the \(3\text{ l}\) container until the \(3\text{ l}\) container is full:

\[
(5,2,3)
\]

3. Pour the \(3\text{ l}\) container back into the \(10\text{ l}\) container:

\[
(8,2,0)
\]

4. Pour the remaining \(2\text{ l}\) from the \(5\text{ l}\) container into the \(3\text{ l}\) container:

\[
(8,0,2)
\]

5. Pour from the \(10\text{ l}\) container into the \(5\text{ l}\) container until it is full:

\[
(3,5,2)
\]

6. Pour from the \(5\text{ l}\) container into the \(3\text{ l}\) container until the \(3\text{ l}\) container is full.  
It already contains \(2\text{ l}\), so it needs \(1\text{ l}\). Thus the \(5\text{ l}\) container is left with

\[
5-1=4\text{ l}.
\]

Final state:

\[
(3,4,3)
\]

So the \(5\text{ l}\) container now contains exactly \(4\text{ l}\) of milk.

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, Martin can measure out exactly }4\text{ l.}}
\]
